# Bellows and the double-acting piston blower (`bellows_piston_blower`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by water_wheel, cam_camshaft, crank_connecting_rod
- Core idea: A fire's heat depends on its air supply; a strong steady blast is what lifts a furnace from red to white heat and makes iron run. A simple bellows blows only on the closing stroke, so smiths use two in turn. The Chinese box bellows blows on both strokes: a long wooden box with a piston packed with feathers or soft paper, an inlet flap valve at each end, and an air channel along the side with a swinging flap leading to one nozzle. Push or pull, one side fills while the other delivers. Worked by a water wheel through cams or a crank, bellows give the continuous blast a blast furnace needs; later, cast-iron blowing cylinders replace leather.
- Pitfalls:
  - No inlet valve, so the bellows sucks flame and hot gas back from the fire
  - A puffing, interrupted blast, which will not hold smelting heat
  - Leather that dries and cracks, or a nozzle that reaches into the fire without a clay tuyere
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – pot bellows with skin covers; earlier smelters used blowpipes; egypt: c. 1450 BC – foot-worked pot bellows in the tomb of Rekhmire; china: 31 AD – Du Shi's water-powered blowers for iron furnaces; double-acting piston bellows certain by the Song (Needham argues for the 4th c. BC from texts; disputed); africa: 1st millennium BC onward – bowl and bag bellows in iron smelting; also tall natural-draught furnaces without bellows; americas: pre-Columbian – no bellows; Andean smelters use blowpipes and wind-blown furnaces (huayras); europe: c. 13th–14th c. – water-powered bellows make the blast furnace possible; c. 1550 wooden box bellows at Nuremberg; 1760s Smeaton's cast-iron blowing cylinders at Carron
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
  - Donald B. Wagner, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 5 Part 11: Ferrous Metallurgy (2008)
